mentl/0df802c:
The deepest unification yet: every compiler tool is a handler
on the same 4-stage effect pipeline.

Pipeline effect ops:
  tokenize(source) → tokens
  parse_source(tokens) → ast
  infer(ast) → (env, subst, counter)    ← NEW
  generate(checked, ast) → chunk

6 handlers, same pipeline:
  compile_standard    — just compile
  compile_teaching    — infer + types + ONE gradient suggestion
  compile_explaining  — infer + full Why Engine reasoning chains
  compile_documenting — infer + typed signatures (lux doc)
  compile_checking    — infer only, no codegen (lux check)
  compile_tracing     — all intermediate representations

REPL modes:
  :normal :teach :why :trace :quit

Meta-compiler demo shows 5 handlers on same source:
  standard → 5
  teaching → [teach] types: x: Int, then 5
  explaining → WHY: Add requires numeric args ← literals
  documenting → let x: Int
  checking → ✓ type check passed

Gradient engine: suggests ONE annotation per compile.
Display helpers: compact, why (reasoning), doc (signatures).

Same pipeline. Same inference. Five tools.

noodles/0df8531:
midiToFreq minted a Tone.Frequency per triggered note and sixteenth()
a Tone.Time per note stack — the playSampleHit allocation class one
layer up. Both are now plain arithmetic. The swap is bit-exact, proven
at the formula instead of the render (renders carry ~-67 dB of inherent
nondeterminism, so byte-comparing them proves nothing): the double
reciprocal reproduces Tone's toFrequency() path exactly across midi
-12..140, and 15/bpm equals Time("16n").toSeconds() bitwise across
40..220 BPM (.tmp/perf-formula-oracle.mjs). Honest scale, measured
over 15 s of playback (.tmp/perf-tonechurn.mjs): this removes ~45
object constructions a second — ours — while Tone's own internals
still mint ~5,300/s converting times inside triggerAttackRelease and
the clock, which is where the remaining churn lives and stays until a
Tone 15 evaluation says otherwise.
noodles/0debf09:
The dropdown was the whole sound space: four hand-tuned presets per
track. They are now the CORNERS of a continuous space — each melodic
track hosts four synth layers, oscillator and envelope fixed to their
corner, and a patch {x, y} crossfades them with equal-power bilinear
weights while the shared tone controls (filter in log space, drive,
chorus) blend numerically. Corners keep their identity; the space
between inherits their calibration. Layers under 2% weight are muted
and never triggered, so parked-at-a-corner costs what one synth did.

On top, one color insert per track (drums included): tape wobble,
a waveshaper bit-quantizer (Tone's real BitCrusher is worklet-based
and renders silent inside Tone.Offline — the export must match live),
phaser, tremolo with duty-cycle makeup, and a tempo-synced filter wob.
Amount and motion drive each; motion rates quantize to the grid and
chase tempo changes.

Presets survive as names for the corners: the old preset API snaps to
a corner, reads back the dominant one, and the register rules (deep
bass octave folding) key off it. renderOffline applies the same patch
state through the same appliers, so exports carry the morphs.

One Tone.js landmine documented in blood: PolySynth's constructor
volume is baked into each lazily-created VOICE, while later .volume
writes only reach the output node — they stack. Layers construct at
the track source level and the output node carries only the morph
weight; the first draft double-counted the source and dropped every
driveless preset by up to 7 dB (drive stages self-leveled the rest,
which is what gave it away).
